Ephys toolbox to match single units (electrophysiology) either within the same recording (oversplits) or across recordings, by using spatial position and waveform-based parameters - both standard and unstandard metrics to the field.

This toolbox was initially created between August 2022-January 2023 by Enny H. van Beest as a tool to match units across multiple recording(day)s, and/or merge oversplit units within the same day. The toolbox was further optimized between February-October 2023 in collaboration with Célian Bimbard.

## Tracking neurons across days with high-density probes

Imagine trying to understand the brain’s activity over time—an incredibly complex and dynamic process that happens at different speeds.

To solve this problem, we developed a pipeline called UnitMatch, which operates after spike sorting. Before applying UnitMatch, the user spike sorts each recording independently using their preferred algorithm. UnitMatch then deploys a naive Bayes classifier on the units’ average waveform in each recording and tracks units across recordings, assigning a probability to each match.

We tested UnitMatch on sequences of Neuropixels recordings from multiple regions of the mouse brain and found that it reliably tracked neurons across weeks. Its performance compares well to the concatenated method and to curation by human experts, while being much faster and applicable to longer sequences of recordings.

Because UnitMatch relies only on each unit’s spike waveform, and not on any functional properties, it can be used to test whether these properties change over time. Indeed, while units can maintain firing properties such as inter-spike interval (ISI) distribution10,11,12,19,20,28,29 and sensory, cognitive or motor correlates11,13,14,15,24,28,29,31,38, the stability of these properties cannot be assumed. ### 3.1 Cross-session unit tracking and within-session controls

Before matching units across days, we test how well their spike waveforms identify them within one recording. We extract features from each recording half using the released code and probe geometry (82 time samples and 384 channels per half). Units with the same sorting label in both halves serve as presumed matches. We compare waveform shape alone with shape and spatial position. In five-fold cross-validation, we estimate the matching thresholds on the training folds. For each held-out unit, we test two sets of ten possible matches from the other recording half. One set contains the presumed match and nine alternatives. The other contains ten alternatives, allowing us to test whether the procedure rejects all of them. The waveform score is centered-waveform correlation. The combined score subtracts $0.5(d_{\rm centroid}/100)^{2}$, where $d_{\rm centroid}$ is the distance between amplitude-weighted waveform centers in released channel-coordinate units. For each training unit, we randomly draw ten units with different labels and record their largest score. The cutoff is the empirical 95th percentile of these maxima across training units, rounded up to an observed value. We accept the highest-scoring held-out comparison only if its score exceeds the cutoff.

###### Abstract

A difference in recorded firing rate across days may reflect a change in neuronal activity, missed spikes or recording a different neuron. We present a statistical approach that combines neuron tracking with Bayesian estimates of stationary mean recorded firing rates. Bounds under assumed differences in spike detection connect recorded rates to biological rate changes. We assess recording loss and uncertainty in rate changes in simulations, and count-model fit in recordings. We also compare two transformer estimators with Gaussian and flow variational inference under a shared temporal negative-binomial model. Flow variational inference agrees most closely with reference posteriors, while predictive performance varies across mice. Rate-change intervals contain true simulated changes less often than intended. In UnitMatch recordings from five mice, some inferred changes remain supported when spike detection is allowed to differ between days; others depend on equal detection. These interpretations require a correct neuron match. The approach identifies which inferred rate changes remain supported under specified recording assumptions and where uncertainty limits interpretation.

Longitudinal electrophysiology, neuron tracking, recording uncertainty, in-context learning, variational inference, count models

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11978519/)Abstract

Neural activity spans multiple time scales, from milliseconds to months. Its evolution can be recorded with chronic high-density arrays such as Neuropixels probes, which can measure each spike at tens of sites and record hundreds of neurons. These probes produce vast amounts of data that require different approaches for tracking neurons across recordings. Here, to meet this need, we developed UnitMatch, a pipeline that operates after spike sorting, based only on each unit’s average spike waveform. We tested UnitMatch in Neuropixels recordings from the mouse brain, where it tracked neurons across weeks. Across the brain, neurons had distinctive inter-spike interval distributions. Their correlations with other neurons remained stable over weeks. In the visual cortex, the neurons’ selectivity for visual stimuli remained similarly stable. In the striatum, however, neuronal responses changed across days during learning of a task. UnitMatch is thus a promising tool to reveal both invariance and plasticity in neural activity across days.

keenable.snippet:
We compare UnitMatch with concatenated sorting, which sorts both recording days together. Agreement supports a proposed match, although errors in the two procedures may be related because they use the same recordings.

A proposed match contains one group from each day that may come from the same neuron. We call this a *candidate pair*.

We check the waveform matches against *concatenated sorting*, which sorts both days’ recordings together. In each session, we link separately sorted units to jointly sorted units by counting their shared spike events. Ambiguous events remain in the denominators of the overlap fractions. We vary the spike-pairing tolerance over 0, 1 and 3 samples (0, 33.3 and 100 microseconds at 30 kHz). We also vary the minimum overlap fraction over 0.5, 0.7 and 0.9. The overlap fraction is the proportion of one unit’s spike events also assigned to the other unit. A link must meet the threshold in both directions and be the unique largest overlap for both units. A separately sorted unit from each day linked to the same jointly sorted unit forms a candidate pair. We keep candidates from any of the nine settings or either waveform analysis. We call a pair *tracking-concordant* when the initial UnitMatch analysis and concatenated sorting both support it.

Among tracking-concordant pairs, 14 met the Gaussian AR criterion at q=1, one at q∈[0.8,1.25] and zero at q∈[0.5,2]. The pair meeting the criterion at q∈[0.8,1.25] had identical analysis windows and concatenated-sorting support under one of nine settings.

What Is the Couples Match and Who Should Consider It?The Couples Match allows two applicants to link their Rank Order Lists(ROLs)so the NRMP algorithm treats them as a single combined unit.When the algorithm runs,it moves down your paired list and matches you to the highest-ranked combination where both of you are accepted.If a program wants Partner A,but Partner B's paired program at rank#4 has already filled its spots,the algorithm skips that pair and looks at rank#5.

seltz.snippet:
You are given a list of non-negative integers `nums`. Arrange them in some order and write them one after another, with no separators, to form a single number. For example, the order `[34, 5]` produces `345` and the order `[5, 34]` produces `534`.

Return the largest number that can be produced this way. Because it can be far too long for any integer type, return it as a **string**. The result must not have leading zeros, so if every possible arrangement is made only of zeros, return `"0"`.

### Example 1

**Input:** nums = [34,5] **Output:** "534" **Why:** 5 goes first, then 34, giving 534 rather than 345.

### Example 2

**Input:** nums = [8,90,1,84,9] **Output:** "9908841" **Why:** 9 comes before 90 because 990 > 909, and 8 comes before 84 because 884 > 848. The order 9, 90, 8, 84, 1 gives 9908841.

### Example 3

**Input:** nums = [0,0,0] **Output:** "0" **Why:** All values are zero, so the answer is the single digit "0", not "000".

### Constraints

- `1 <= nums.length <= 100`
- `0 <= nums[i] <= 109`

Pattern Path · **Intervals & Greedy** · problem 115 of 169

Sorting by numeric value fails (10 would come before 9). Sorting the decimal strings in descending order also fails for some pairs: compare 3 and 30. Why?

Focus on just two numbers `a` and `b`. Which one should come first in the final answer?

Put `a` before `b` exactly when the string `a + b` is larger than `b + a`. Sort with that comparison and join. Watch for an all-zero input.

**Target:** O(n log n · d), d = digits per number time, O(n · d) extra space.

### Start simple

Try every permutation, concatenate, and keep the largest: O(n!·L) time for n numbers of total length L.

### The key idea

Decide the order one pair at a time. For two numbers written as strings `a` and `b`, the only two ways to place them next to each other are `a+b` and `b+a`. Both have the same length, so comparing them as strings tells you which order is better for that pair.

A **data type** specifies the kind of value. The type int represents an integer, char represents one UTF-16 code unit, and boolean represents true or false. UTF-16 is a representation of Unicode text; Unicode assigns codes to characters. A code unit is one storage unit in that representation.

seltz.snippet: A retailer's database must join a 500-million-row `orders` table with a 50-million-row `customers` table on `customer_id`. Neither table fits in memory. Nested-loop join, even the block-oriented variant, degrades badly here. Without a usable index, it must rescan the inner relation once per outer block. We need an algorithm that touches each page a bounded, small number of times, regardless of how large the relations are. It should turn the combinatorial matching problem into a simple linear scan. ultimate.title: Tracking neurons across days with high-density probes
ultimate.snippet:
Its evolution can be recorded with chronic high-density arrays such as Neuropixels probes, which can measure each spike at tens of sites and record hundreds of neurons. These probes produce vast amounts of data that require different approaches for tracking neurons across recordings. Here, to meet this need, we developed UnitMatch, a pipeline that operates after spike sorting, based only on each unit’s average spike waveform. We tested UnitMatch in Neuropixels recordings from the mouse brain, where it tracked neurons across weeks. Across the brain, neurons had distinctive inter-spike interval distributions. Their correlations with other neurons remained stable over weeks. In the visual cortex, the neurons’ selectivity for visual stimuli remained similarly stable. In the striatum, however, neuronal responses changed across days during learning of a task. UnitMatch is thus a promising tool to reveal both invariance and plasticity in neural activity across days.

The current methods for matching neurons across days, however, cannot process the vast amounts of data produced by sequences of recordings with high-density probes such as Neuropixels. For example, an established method relies on concatenating two recordings and spike sorting the resulting file[30](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1038/s41592-024-02440-1#ref-CR30),[31](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1038/s41592-024-02440-1#ref-CR31). This method can work well for pairs of recordings but becomes unwieldy for longer sequences. It does not scale to the dozens of recordings that may be obtained across weeks or months.
To solve this problem, we developed a pipeline called UnitMatch, which operates after spike sorting. Before applying UnitMatch, the user spike sorts each recording independently using their preferred algorithm. UnitMatch then deploys a naive Bayes classifier on the units’ average waveform in each recording and tracks units across recordings, assigning a probability to each match.

ultimate.title: Density-based longitudinal neuron tracking in high-density electrophysiological recordings
ultimate.snippet:
Several methods leverage these high-density recordings to track neurons across sessions. One straightforward approach concatenates pairs of sessions and sorts them jointly.^3^ This has the advantage of applying the same spike-sorting standard (e.g., the same templates in Kilosort), but its success depends on motion correction, which requires sufficiently similar activity patterns between the paired sessions. In practice, this approach also adds substantial burden to data processing, analysis, and storage, limiting scalability. Two independent alternatives have been proposed: the earth mover’s distance (EMD) method, which finds an optimal matching between units across sessions by minimizing a combined cost of physical distance and waveform dissimilarity,^18^ and UnitMatch, which uses a similarity score calibrated from within-session data to identify putative matches and non-matches across sessions, which are then used to train a naive Bayes classifier.^7^ Both methods operate on pairwise comparisons of sessions.
